title: A half plus a third
hook: Add the tops, add the bottoms: 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5. Does the picture agree?

knows: unit fractions as one piece of a whole cut into equal pieces (1/2, 1/3)
doesNotKnow: why fractions with different bottoms must be cut into same-size pieces before they can be added

misconception: 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5: add the tops and add the bottoms.
objective: The learner can re-cut a half and a third into sixths (3 + 2) and explain that 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, and that 2/5 is less than the half alone.

claims.text: Cut into sixths, the half is 3 pieces and the third is 2, so 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6.
In twelfths the half is 6 pieces and the third 4, 10/12, the same length as 5/6.
2/5 is less than 1/2 alone, so 1/2 + 1/3 cannot be 2/5.
claims.source: 2/5 = 0.4 < 0.5 = 1/2 (node). Adding a positive third cannot make the total smaller than the half.

claims.text: In fourths the third ends mid-piece, and in fifths neither the half nor the third ends on a cut line.
claims.source: A piece 1/d ends on a cut line of n equal pieces only when d divides n (Demo.tsx fits): 3 ∤ 4; 2 ∤ 5 and 3 ∤ 5 (the third ends at 5/6 = 25/30, not a multiple of 1/5).

claims.text: Fractions can be added once both are cut into pieces of the same size.
claims.source: a/b + c/d = (ad + cb)/bd: rewrite both over a common denominator, then add numerators (standard school arithmetic).

recall.question: What is 1/3 + 1/4?
recall.why: Cut both into twelfths: 1/3 = 4/12 and 1/4 = 3/12, so 7/12. 2/7 is less than the third alone.
